n: Divorce existed in Israel, but it required a written certificate. The document protected the woman by proving she was free to remarry. Jesus later said Moses allowed this because of hardened hearts.

f.g: Hebrew “a matter of nakedness” — something shameful; its meaning was debated by later rabbis.

n: Once divorced, she was legally free to marry someone else.
If the second marriage also ended, by divorce or death…
…the first husband could not take her back. This rule likely discouraged hasty divorces and treating wives as exchangeable.

f.g: After she has been joined to another man.

n: A newlywed husband was excused from military service and public duties for a full year so he could build a happy marriage. God cares about joy in marriage.
A lender couldn’t take a family’s millstone as collateral, because without it they couldn’t grind grain for daily bread.

f.w: the nether or the upper millstone
f.g: The lower or upper stone of a hand mill.

n: Kidnapping a fellow Israelite to enslave or sell him was a capital crime — as Joseph’s brothers had done to him.

f.g: Treats him as goods to sell.

n: For serious skin diseases, the people must carefully follow the priests’ instructions given in Leviticus.

f.g: Various skin diseases, not only modern leprosy.

n: Remember Miriam: when she spoke against Moses, she was struck with this disease and shut outside the camp for seven days.
A lender couldn’t barge into a borrower’s home to seize collateral, protecting the poor person’s dignity and privacy.

f.g: To take the security for the loan.

n: The lender must wait outside and let the borrower bring out what he chose.
If a poor man gave his cloak as collateral, the lender couldn’t keep it overnight.

f.w: thou shalt not sleep with his pledge

n: Return the cloak by sunset so he has something to sleep in. Showing mercy counts as righteousness before God.

f.w: it shall be righteousness unto thee

f.g: Clothing, here the outer cloak used as a blanket.

n: Don’t exploit poor hired workers, whether Israelite or foreign.
Pay wages the same day. A poor worker depends on it to eat tonight, and God hears his cry.

f.w: neither shall the sun go down upon it

n: Each person is responsible for his own crimes. Parents and children cannot be executed for each other’s sins.

f.w: every man shall be put to death for his own sin

n: Justice for the vulnerable: don’t twist cases against foreigners or orphans, and don’t take a widow’s clothing as collateral.
The motive again: remember that you were slaves and God redeemed you.

f.w: the LORD thy God redeemed thee thence

n: If a bundle of grain was forgotten in the field, leave it for the poor. This is how Ruth was able to glean in Boaz’s fields.

f.g: A bundle of cut grain stalks.

f.w: for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow

n: When beating olives from the trees, don’t go back for a second pass — leave the rest for the poor.

f.g: Olives were harvested by striking branches with sticks.

n: Grape harvest too: don’t strip the vines clean. Leave the remainder for those in need.

f.g: Gather leftover crops after the main harvest.

n: The chapter closes by repeating the reason: Israel’s memory of slavery should make them compassionate.
